prime.problem: A data agent says "Q3 net revenue for EMEA was $48.3M." Without the path behind that number, nobody can tell which revenue definition, table, date range or filters it used, whose access it ran under, or what it quietly assumed. A wrong number and a right one look identical.
prime.fits: The trust card of the data-agents course. It is the data-agent version of the claim chain from 'Done' is a chain of states, and it applies Authority only narrows to answers built from a warehouse.
expect: the analyst loop (plan, inspect, execute, observe, validate, revise, explain)
the run receipt (what ran, who as, what was assumed or denied)
the context manifest (why that query ran)
same effective access as the requester
shared analytical memory as an open consent question
prime.goal: Write the receipt for any data-agent answer, say which failure each field would expose, and explain why even a complete receipt cannot tell you the number is right.

attend: Which step of the analyst loop changed the EMEA query, and where on the receipt does that change show up?
Why does the receipt need two identities, and what goes wrong when only the acting service account is recorded?
Why does the denial line on the receipt describe the limit on the answer instead of naming the restricted table?
Which claim-chain link does a receipt fail to witness, and which new question does a data run add to the chain?
What does the context manifest record that the SQL alone can't, and who is it written for?
What would have to be true before Meta-style reuse of a colleague's query history counts as authorized?

must: Real analysis loops (plan → inspect → execute → observe → validate → revise → explain) → each step can change the number (a zero-row result forces a new filter, a default picks the quarter) → each step must leave a line in the receipt → otherwise the answer is a plausible sentence with a number attached

The tool runs as a service identity, not the requester → the service account can usually read more → a correct query can return data the requester may not know → the receipt records requester and actor separately, plus the policy decision and denied sources → a successful query is not proof of an authorized answer

A receipt shows what ran, who as and what was assumed → it never compares the number to the truth → a complete receipt can document the wrong canonical table chosen under the right permissions → a receipt makes a run explainable; only an eval says it was right

Saving a correction or reusing a colleague's history is a data write and a read across people → if scope widens automatically, one analyst's filter or confidential context reaches others → shared memory needs an owner, provenance, a review step and revocation; whether Meta's colleague-history feature has these is not public
elevated: The receipt references governed data (result IDs, hashes, bounded samples) instead of copying it → it stays small and doesn't become a second, less governed warehouse → but it is still sensitive (questions, identities, SQL, destinations), so it needs scoped access, tamper resistance and retention

The context manifest keeps rejected and superseded candidates with reason codes → when two runs give different answers you can see whether ranking, permissions or a stale source changed → without it the divergence is visible but the cause isn't reproducible
reference: Part 6's 16-item minimum receipt list (requesting and acting identity, policy decision and version, sources considered and denied, context IDs or hashes, tools, SQL, tables and protected fields, limits and masking, result references, assumptions, fallbacks, memory reads and writes, destination, model and workflow version)
Part 1's 9-item user-facing receipt as recapped in Part 3
the memory scopes: session, personal, team or domain, global
the illustrative identifiers on the card (r_emea_q3, ctx_41b, q_7f3a, svc-data-agent)

compress.prompt: Card closed: sketch the EMEA receipt as five labelled groups (answer, what ran, who it ran as, why this source, what it assumed and sent). Under each group write the failure it exposes. Then mark the one claim-chain link no group can witness.
checklist: answer + result link; question as interpreted (metric definition, quarter, region)
what ran: SQL, tables, checks, the revision after zero rows → exposes evidence-free answers
who it ran as: requester vs acting identity, policy decision, denied sources → exposes a privilege bridge
why this source: the context manifest's chosen and rejected candidates → exposes a deprecated table winning on similarity
assumed and sent: surfaced defaults, memory reads and writes, destination → exposes silent defaults, scope creep, unapproved publishing
effect verified (is the number right?) stays unwitnessed: that is an eval's job

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between a receipt and a context manifest, using the EMEA run, and say who reads each.
answer: receipt: user-facing record of what ran, who as, what was assumed, denied or swapped
context manifest: operator-facing record of why that query ran (candidates, reason codes, rejected sources, bundle hash, versions)
in the EMEA run the receipt shows the SQL and defaults; the manifest shows that rev_dash_legacy lost because it was deprecated, not on similarity
Part 3: a query link proves what ran; a context manifest proves why it ran

retrieve.q: Walk through Part 6's opening run (42,871 rows, a chart that matched last quarter) and say which receipt fields would have exposed the problem.
answer: the SQL compiled and the result looked right, so the what-ran section is clean
the requester couldn't access the customer-level table; the service identity could
recording requester and actor separately, plus the policy decision, shows the actor read beyond the requester's policy
a policy layer re-applying the requester's access on every call would have denied the table and logged the denial

retrieve.q: Your security team wants every run's full result set and retrieved documents stored in the trace "for completeness". What do you argue, and what do you store instead?
answer: a full copy turns the audit store into a second, less governed warehouse
the receipt is sensitive anyway (questions, identities, SQL, destinations)
store stable IDs, hashes, policy decisions and bounded samples that point back to governed systems
give the receipt its own scoped access, tamper-resistant storage and retention rule

retrieve.q: The canonical table is denied, and an authorized weekly summary exists. When should the agent use it silently, use it and disclose, or stop and ask?
answer: never silently: a fallback can keep authorization but change grain, population, filters, freshness or definition
compare the two on those dimensions first
disclose and name the limit when the substitute answers nearly the same question
ask when it answers a materially different question: a transparent limited answer beats a confident answer to another question

compare.q: The claim chain checks a coding agent's "done"; the receipt backs a data agent's number. Which link does each leave to an outside verifier, and what does the data run add that a coding run never needs?
answer: same: both split one claim into separately witnessed states, and both leave "effect verified" to something outside the agent
coding: the checker reruns the tests on the files you accept; data: an eval compares the number with a golden result
the data run adds an authorization axis: a correct, verified number can still be one the requester may not know
failure: a coding run fails by a false success claim; a data run can also fail by being right and unauthorized, or explainable and wrong

compare.q: Authority only narrows sets the rule; the receipt records whether the rule held. What does each one do, and how does each fail on its own?
answer: the envelope carries the requester's authority into every tool call and enforces it at run time
the receipt is after-the-fact evidence: requester, actor, policy decision, denied sources
envelope without receipt: enforcement you can't audit or debug, and denials that show up only as "I could not answer"
receipt without envelope: a precise record of a privilege bridge that already happened

predict.q: Next quarter the finance team changes the net_revenue definition to also subtract chargebacks. Maya re-asks the same question, and the stored receipt from this quarter is still on file. Which fields of the old receipt tell you why the two answers differ, and what does the receipt still not tell you?
predict.answer: The interpreted-as line (metric definition and its registry version), the context manifest's source versions, and the model and workflow versions would show the definition changed between runs, so the difference is explainable. What neither receipt says is which number is right for Maya's purpose, or whether the new definition was applied consistently across tables: that needs a golden question re-run against the new contract, which is the next card's job.

apply.task: Run python3 code/receipts.py. Then build a fifth receipt, dict(EMEA, memory_write="global"): the EMEA run, but the agent saved Maya's correction straight to application-wide memory. Predict the checker's verdict before running. Then add a rule for Part 6's failure 5 (personal memory becomes global) so this receipt is flagged.
apply.done: Before your change, the fifth receipt prints only explainable (not proof it is right), because no rule reads memory_write. After it, the same receipt prints a memory-scope flag, while the original EMEA receipt still prints only "explainable".
apply.hint: A write wider than "personal" is fine only if the receipt also shows it went through review, so check both a scope field and something like promotion_reviewed.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: what the fifth receipt would print, or which old-receipt fields explain a definition change?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the actor must be recorded separately from the requester, or why a complete receipt still isn't a correctness check?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: analyst-loop step → receipt line, or receipt line → the failure it exposes?
In a data or coding agent you've built, which of the receipt's groups is recorded by nothing today?
If a colleague's query history were reused as context for you, what would you want to see on your receipt?
